summary:
SOL CREW – Mars Outpost is a free, co-op browser game that trains junior astronauts aged 7–12 by letting them live on Mars instead of reading about it. One to four players run Jezero Outpost together and must keep three things alive until the supply ship lands: power, air and food. Kids wipe dust off solar panels, fix pumps, grow potatoes and lettuce, make oxygen with an Exchanger modelled on NASA's MOXIE, and race to the storm shelter when a solar flare hits.

The challenge comes from real science. Solar storms are real flares from NASA's DONKI space-weather database, the radio delay to Earth is calculated from today's real planet positions, and every new action unlocks a short "Did you know?" card with a real NASA photo and a one-question quiz.

Space is exciting, but big numbers and textbook words make it hard for children to understand. SOL CREW turns those ideas into choices kids can feel: if the battery runs out, the lights go dark; if no one farms, the crew goes hungry. It runs on any laptop or tablet, with no download or account, in English and Chinese.
details:
What it does
SOL CREW – Mars Outpost is a 2D co-op survival game for kids aged 7–12. Players pick an astronaut, and each crew role has its own skill: engineers repair machines faster and botanists grow more food. Together they run a Mars base for 5 sols (Mars days). The goal is simple to say and hard to do: keep Power, Air and Food above zero until the supply ship lands.

How it works
Solar panels only work in daylight, so the battery has to last through the night. Every job is a short, touch-friendly mini-game: scrubbing dust off solar panels, drilling ice for water, planting and watering crops, tightening leaking pipes, rebooting the computer with a code, and pulling the lever on the Exchanger, which turns power into oxygen just like NASA's MOXIE experiment. Things also go wrong: machines wear out, dust builds up and solar storms arrive. When the battery runs out, the base really goes dark, machines stop and emergency lamps flash, and when the crew is hungry or the air is low, the astronauts slow down and show it. The challenge is built on real data. Solar storms are real flares from NASA's DONKI space-weather database (live when online, otherwise famous archive events such as September 2017 and May 2024), and the Earth–Mars radio delay and Mars season are calculated from today's real planet positions using JPL data, so messages to Earth take real minutes. The first time a kid does something new, a "Did you know?" card appears with a real NASA photo, one short fact and a one-question quiz that earns a science star. Stars buy upgrades such as an extra solar row, a dust shield, a fission reactor, hydroponics and a shelter water wall, and every upgrade visibly changes the base. At the end, a mission graph shows Power, Air and Food over time, with tips on what to try next.

Benefits and intended impact
SOL CREW turns abstract ideas like energy budgets, life support, radiation, food growth and communication delay into cause and effect that children can see and feel. Co-op play builds teamwork, because friends must split jobs and talk to each other just like a real crew; kids can also play solo with a helper crew, or online with a 4-letter room code. The game is free, with no download, no account and no ads, and it runs in a browser on laptops, Chromebooks and tablets, so schools and families can use it right away. It is bilingual (English and Simplified Chinese), with large text and an optional read-aloud mode for younger players.

Tools and technologies
The game is written in JavaScript (ES modules). All art is drawn in code with HTML5 Canvas 2D, so there are no image files, and all music and sound effects are generated in code with the Web Audio API. We used Vite to build the project, PeerJS (WebRTC) for online co-op, and GitHub Pages with GitHub Actions for hosting. The demo video was recorded from the real game with Playwright and edited with FFmpeg.

How it is creative
Instead of a quiz with a game wrapped around it, in SOL CREW the science is the game rules. Dust really lowers solar output, night really drains the battery, and a real NASA-recorded solar flare really sends the crew running to the shelter. Each lesson appears right after the action it explains, so kids learn "why" at the exact moment they care about the answer.

Factors we considered
We kept the reading level age-appropriate with short sentences, added colour-blind-friendly icons next to every bar, and included three difficulty settings (calm, normal and hard). We made sure the game stays fun even when the network is down by falling back to archive data. For kid safety, there is no chat, no account and no personal data. For scientific accuracy, every fact in the game has a listed source.
